short: Arkansas has no dedicated AI act, but its 2025 session passed five AI-specific laws on deepfakes, AI-generated CSAM, publicity rights, and government AI use, and older consumer, privacy, and insurance statutes already reach AI conduct.
title: Arkansas AI Laws
subtitle: No omnibus AI act, but 2025 brought deepfake, AI-CSAM, publicity-rights, and government-use laws, plus older statutes that already reach AI.
body_html:
Arkansas has no omnibus AI act like Colorado's or Texas's, but calling the state unregulated on AI would be wrong. The 2025 regular session produced five separate AI laws covering deepfakes, AI-generated child sexual abuse material, publicity rights, content ownership, and government AI use, while a separate push to regulate AI in election ads failed. Older consumer protection, data breach, and insurance rules already reach a lot of AI-driven conduct in the state.

What the legislature did

The 95th General Assembly's 2025 regular session was Arkansas's first real AI legislative moment. HB1958 (Rep. Stephen Meeks, Sen. Jane English) passed the House 93-0 and Senate 35-0 and became Act 848, requiring every public entity to adopt a written policy on authorized AI use, keep a human in the loop on final decisions, train employees, and publish the policy. HB1529 (Meeks, with more than 40 co-sponsors) became Act 827, making it a Class A misdemeanor, a Class D felony on repeat, to create or distribute a deepfake showing an identifiable person nude or engaged in sexual activity without consent, plus a civil claim against creators or platforms that promote such material. HB1877 (Meeks and Sen. Joshua Bryant) became Act 977, amending the 1979 Protection of Children Against Exploitation Act to define "computer generated" and "indistinguishable" material, closing off any defense that AI-generated CSAM does not depict a real child. HB1071 (Rep. Scott Richardson, Bryant) became Act 159, the first of the batch signed, amending the 2016 Frank Broyles Publicity Rights Protection Act to cover unauthorized commercial use of an AI-generated voice or likeness. HB1876 (Richardson, Bryant) became Act 927, giving default ownership of AI-generated content and trained models to whoever supplied the inputs, unless it infringes someone else's copyright or was made within the scope of employment, in which case the employer owns it.

Not everything moved. Two election-deepfake bills, HB1141 (Richardson, criminalizing "deceptive and injurious media" in campaigns) and HB1041 (a bipartisan bill from Minority Leader Andrew Collins setting civil fines for malicious election deepfakes), both died in House committee at sine die adjournment without a floor vote. HB1816, which would have restricted AI use by health providers and insurers in clinical decisions and records, was withdrawn by its sponsor in April 2025. Arkansas's quieter 2023 session produced no comparable AI-specific legislation.

What already applies without a dedicated AI act

Several existing Arkansas laws reach AI use even though they predate it. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act bars unconscionable, false, or deceptive acts in commerce, broad enough for the Attorney General to use against a company whose AI tool misrepresents what it does or how it handles customer data. The Personal Information Protection Act defines "personal information" to include biometric identifiers such as fingerprints, voiceprints, and iris or retina scans, so a company training or running AI on Arkansans' biometric data faces the Act's security-safeguard and 45-day breach-notice duties if that data is exposed. And Insurance Department Bulletin 13-2024, issued July 2024, tells every licensed insurer that using AI does not excuse it from the state's unfair trade practices and anti-discrimination rules, and that insurers need a written AI governance program covering model testing, bias monitoring, vendor oversight, and consumer notice.

What the Attorney General has done

Attorney General Tim Griffin has been active on AI policy, without any publicly known AI-specific enforcement case yet. In September 2023 he joined a 54-attorney-general coalition asking Congress to fund a commission studying how AI is used to exploit children, citing tools that generate new child sexual abuse material from real photos or graft children's faces onto abusive content. In July 2025 he welcomed the Senate's 99-1 vote stripping a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI regulation from federal budget legislation, arguing states are best positioned to regulate AI, protect consumers, and prosecute AI-generated CSAM. In May 2026 his office opened an "Emerging Issues Series" event on AI in legal practice for more than 400 attorneys, telling them AI has moved from optional to required.

What this means

Arkansas residents and businesses should not read the absence of a Colorado-style AI act as an absence of exposure. Deepfake pornography, AI-generated CSAM, and unauthorized commercial use of someone's AI-cloned voice or image are all now specific crimes or civil claims under 2025 law, public agencies must have a written AI policy on file, and general consumer protection, biometric privacy, and insurance rules already apply to AI systems the moment they touch an Arkansan's money, data, or coverage decisions, regardless of whether the word "artificial intelligence" appears in the statute.
